subject: Vocabulary
topic: Figures of Speech — Similes, Metaphors, and More

questions.stem: Identify the figure of speech: 'Life is a journey with no map.'
questions.explanation: B is correct. METAPHOR = a direct comparison stating one thing IS another, without 'like' or 'as.' 'Life is a journey' = metaphor. SIMILE uses 'like/as': 'Life is LIKE a journey.' Key distinction: Simile (comparison) uses 'like/as'; Metaphor (equation) states directly.

questions.stem: Identify the figure of speech: 'The wind whispered through the trees.'
questions.explanation: C is correct. PERSONIFICATION = attributing human characteristics or actions to non-human entities. 'Wind WHISPERED' = wind given the human ability to whisper. Other examples: 'the sun smiled', 'the trees danced', 'time flies', 'death knocked at his door.'

questions.stem: Identify the figure of speech: 'She runs as fast as the wind.'
questions.explanation: B is correct. SIMILE = comparison using 'like' or 'as.' 'As fast as the wind' uses 'as...as' → simile. Common simile patterns: 'as bright as the sun', 'like a fish out of water', 'ran like the wind', 'brave as a lion.'

questions.stem: Identify the figure of speech: 'I have told you a million times!'
questions.explanation: C is correct. HYPERBOLE = deliberate extreme exaggeration used for emphasis or dramatic effect. 'A million times' = you clearly haven't said it a million times. Other hyperboles: 'I'm so hungry I could eat a horse', 'this bag weighs a ton', 'I've been waiting forever.'

questions.stem: Identify the figure of speech: 'The pen is mightier than the sword.'
questions.explanation: D is correct. METONYMY = a figure of speech in which a word or phrase is substituted with something closely related. 'Pen' = metonym for writing/intellect/words; 'sword' = metonym for violence/military. The sentence also functions as a comparison, but the primary device is metonymy. Compare: SYNECDOCHE (part for whole: 'all hands on deck'); METONYMY (associated substitute: 'the White House said...').

questions.stem: Identify the figure of speech: 'The silence was deafening.'
questions.explanation: C is correct. OXYMORON = two contradictory or opposite terms placed together for effect. 'Deafening silence' = silence (absence of sound) and deafening (loudly overwhelming) are contradictory. Other oxymorons: 'bitter sweet', 'living death', 'open secret', 'deafeningly quiet', 'cruel kindness.'

questions.stem: Identify the figure of speech: 'Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers.'
questions.explanation: B is correct. ALLITERATION = repetition of the same initial consonant sound in nearby words. 'Peter Piper Picked...Peppers' — all start with /p/. Other examples: 'She sells seashells by the seashore.' ASSONANCE = vowel sound repetition: 'Go slow over the road.'

questions.stem: Identify the figure of speech: 'The fog comes on little cat feet.' (Carl Sandburg)
questions.explanation: B is correct. METAPHOR — the fog is described as if it were a cat, moving on 'little cat feet.' This is an IMPLIED METAPHOR (not explicit: not 'fog is a cat' but 'fog comes on cat feet'). The cat's qualities (silent, soft, stealthy movement) are attributed to the fog. A classic example of metaphor in poetry.

questions.stem: Identify the figure of speech: 'He is as brave as a lion.'
questions.explanation: B is correct. 'As brave as a lion' = SIMILE (explicit comparison using 'as'). Common animal similes: as brave as a lion, as busy as a bee, as fast as a cheetah, as quiet as a mouse, as cunning as a fox, as strong as an ox.

questions.stem: Identify the figure of speech: 'The buzz of the bee filled the garden.'
questions.explanation: B is correct. ONOMATOPOEIA = words that phonetically imitate the sound they describe. 'Buzz' sounds like the sound a bee makes. Other onomatopoeia words: hiss (snake), crash (impact), splash (water), bark (dog), whisper, murmur, crackle, sizzle, moo, meow.
